{#sofl} # Discussion

{#bv14} ⟨待采纳·删除·M. Keller⟩ We have previously published two large, register based cohort studies on the topic of cardiovascular risk factors associated with THA. Periacetabular osteolysis is difficult to study due to its “silent” nature without initial symptoms such as pain, and it takes many years to develop, if ever. There is a common denominator for periacetabular osteolysis and atherosclerosis, which is currently suggested as a long time ongoing low-grade inflammation [@w:w36]. {#w4pi} # Introduction

{#kpx3} Primary osteoarthritis is a multifactorial disease with a low-grade inflammatory component . The end-stage surgical treatment for this condition—arthroplasty surgery—can *per se* trigger other inflammatory processes [@w:w1]. As the implant ages, wear debris is generated, which can lead to inflammatory induction of bone resorption adjacent to the implant, defined as osteolysis. One of the most common explanations is that development of excess wear particles produces a proinflammatory state [@w:w2]. It is widely accepted that particulate debris [@w:w3] is the main cause of this condition. It is also shown that osteolysis can be induced by mechanical stimulus of fluid pressure [@w:w4] The proinflammatory state leads to aggravated osteoclast differentiation and macrophage activation. This process in turn leads to local peri-implant osteolysis and aseptic loosening around the prosthesis components. Computed tomography (CT) of the affected hip is considered gold standard for detection of osteolysis [@w:w5].

{#tws7} Osteolysis and aseptic loosening are the most common reasons for total hip arthroplasty (THA) revision surgery [@w:w6]. The result might be extensive revision surgery [@w:w7]. ops.markdown: A major limitation of the present study is its limited sample size and the availability of only a single baseline measurement of hs-CRP, leukocytes and lipids, which makes causal inference difficult. Repeated measurements would have provided a more precise characterisation of the patients. Nor did we control for the use of statins, a class of drugs clinically used to lower serum lipid levels [@w:w38] and the risk of CVD [@w:w39]; statins also suppress osteoclastic bone resorption and have been associated with favourable effects on bone metabolism and inflammation [@w:w40]. In addition, unaccounted confounders, including lifestyle factors and unmeasured comorbidities, might have influenced the observed outcomes. Prevalence-incidence bias (Neyman bias) may also have been introduced, because patients who died of CVD before the study began would have left the cohort with a less severe cardiovascular risk burden. ECG may no longer be the most reliable predictor of future cardiovascular events, and at the time of the study our hospital did not yet perform calcium-score computed tomography. Blood tests were collected only once, so potential fluctuations were missed, which is an inherent limitation of a cross-sectional design. Lifestyle factors, comorbidities and other medications that may affect cardiovascular outcomes are not always documented in the medical records, which could have influenced the results.
